prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "HCA Healthcare, Inc." (ticker HCA), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "HCA", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: HCA Healthcare, Inc.
markets: Outpatient surgery and ambulatory care (surgery centers, urgent care, freestanding ERs, physician clinics)
Private hospital care in the United Kingdom (HCA Healthcare UK)
Healthcare supply purchasing and revenue-cycle services (HealthTrust, Parallon)

mission.statement: Above all else, we are committed to the care and improvement of human life.
mission.source: HCA Healthcare website, 'Our mission and values' page (hcahealthcare.com)
mission.plain: Taking care of sick people and helping them live better lives comes first.

about.plain: HCA runs hospitals across the United States and some in London. When people get sick or hurt, they go to its emergency rooms, have surgery there, or stay in a hospital bed. It also runs smaller places like surgery centers and urgent-care clinics. It is the biggest hospital company in the US that is owned by shareholders.
about.customers: Patients, with most of the bill paid by health insurers and by government programs like Medicare and Medicaid.
about.everyday: If you have gone to an emergency room or had a baby in Florida, Texas or Tennessee, there is a good chance it was at an HCA hospital.

money.plain: Inpatient care, operations, intensive care, births
Surgery centers, urgent care, imaging, doctor clinics
Private hospitals and clinics, mainly in London

money.part: Data and AI tools for care
money.plain: Using its huge patient data and AI (e.g. with Google Cloud) to make nursing and care more efficient

result.summary: HCA has a real but local advantage: it builds dense networks of hospitals, ERs and surgery centers in fast-growing Sun Belt cities, often holding the No. 1 or No. 2 position, which gives it leverage with insurers, purchasing scale and steady patient flow. Its moat is built on scale and local market density rather than a unique product, and it remains exposed to government payment policy, insurer pushback and labor costs. Its stockholders' deficit and $50.5 billion of debt (Sept 30, 2026) reflect heavy buybacks rather than weakness in the business.

pricingPower.evidence: Revenue rose from $70,603M in 2024 to $75,600M in 2025 (+7.1%), driven mostly by patient volume plus payer mix and rate increases negotiated with commercial insurers. Price gains are limited: in Q3 2026 revenue rose 3.6% to $19,849M, while same-facility revenue per equivalent admission grew only 0.6% and equivalent admissions grew 3.0%, partly because more uninsured patients came in after enhanced ACA exchange subsidies expired (about a $400M hit to Q3 pre-tax income). Medicare and Medicaid rates are set by government, so HCA cannot raise them.

moats.evidence: Most HCA hospitals operate under local brand names (e.g., Medical City, Methodist, HCA Florida), and patients pick by location, doctor and insurer network rather than the HCA name.
Patients can go to another hospital, although physicians with privileges and insurers that include HCA networks find it disruptive to drop a dominant local system.

Dense local networks (hospitals, about 2,500 ambulatory sites of care at end-2025, physician practices, transfer centers) feed referrals to each other and make HCA a must-have for insurer networks in markets like Dallas, Houston, Denver, Nashville and Florida.

With $75.6B of 2025 revenue and 190 hospitals at end-2025, HCA is the largest US investor-owned hospital operator; its HealthTrust group purchasing, Parallon shared services and data platform spread fixed costs over a base far larger than Tenet ($21.3B) or CHS ($12.5B).
Hospital markets support only a few large systems, and state certificate-of-need laws in places like Florida (partly), Tennessee and Virginia limit new entrants.
HCA's model of owned hospitals is the industry norm; nothing about it is hard for rivals to copy because of their own business models.

Decades of standardized operating playbooks, clinical data from tens of millions of patient encounters and tight labor and supply management give HCA consistently higher margins than most for-profit peers (2025 net margin 9.0% vs CHS 4.1%).
Its own nursing school (Galen College of Nursing) and graduate medical education programs help supply staff, but it has no truly exclusive asset.

customers.evidence: Patient volumes keep growing (Q3 2026 same-facility admissions +2.7%, ER visits +5.1%), showing communities keep choosing HCA facilities, but patient reviews of hospitals are mixed and HCA has faced criticism and lawsuits over billing and staffing; there is no published company-wide NPS.

talent.evidence: HCA was named one of Fortune's World's Most Admired Companies for the 12th consecutive year (2026) and runs Galen College of Nursing and large residency programs, but nurse unions have repeatedly protested staffing levels at HCA hospitals and labor shortages remain a constant cost pressure.

product.evidence: Many HCA hospitals earn quality awards and it has deep clinical data, but academic medical centers (e.g., Mayo, Cleveland Clinic) are generally seen as best-in-class for complex care; HCA's strength is consistent, efficient community care.

competitors.name: Tenet Healthcare Corporation
competitors.note: For-profit hospitals and USPI surgery centers; competes head-on in Texas, Florida and other Sun Belt markets.

competitors.name: Universal Health Services, Inc.
competitors.note: Acute-care hospitals in Las Vegas, Texas, Florida and DC area, plus the largest behavioral health network.

competitors.name: Community Health Systems, Inc.
competitors.note: For-profit hospitals in smaller and mid-sized markets, mainly in the South.

competitors.name: Ardent Health, Inc.
competitors.note: For-profit hospital systems in Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico and other mid-sized markets.

competitors.name: AdventHealth
competitors.note: Large nonprofit system and HCA's main rival in Florida (Orlando, Tampa).

competitors.name: Baylor Scott & White Health
competitors.note: Nonprofit system competing with HCA's Medical City network in Dallas-Fort Worth and Central Texas.

competitors.name: Memorial Hermann Health System
competitors.note: Nonprofit competing with HCA Houston Healthcare.

competitors.name: CommonSpirit Health
competitors.note: Large Catholic nonprofit system overlapping in Texas, Colorado, California, Nevada and Tennessee.

competitors.name: Ascension
competitors.note: Catholic nonprofit system overlapping in Texas, Florida, Tennessee (Ascension Saint Thomas in Nashville) and other states.

competitors.name: LifePoint Health
competitors.note: Private-equity-owned (Apollo) operator of community hospitals, mostly in rural and small markets.

competitors.name: Prime Healthcare
competitors.note: Private hospital operator in California and other states.

competitors.name: Surgery Partners, Inc.
competitors.note: Ambulatory surgery centers competing with HCA's outpatient surgery business.

competitors.name: UnitedHealth Group (Optum)
competitors.note: Optum's surgery centers (SCA Health) and physician groups compete for outpatient procedures and steer patients.

competitors.name: Spire Healthcare Group plc
competitors.note: UK private hospital operator competing with HCA Healthcare UK.

marketShare.market: US hospital care spending (approximate estimate: each company's total 2024 revenue divided by CMS's ~$1.6 trillion 2024 national hospital care spending; company revenue includes some non-hospital services)

threats: Expiry of enhanced ACA exchange subsidies at end-2025 is raising uninsured volumes (about a $400M hit to Q3 2026 pre-tax income).
Federal budget law changes to Medicaid, including limits on state directed and supplemental payments that currently benefit HCA.
Medicare rate pressure, sequestration and site-neutral payment reforms that would cut hospital outpatient rates.
Large insurers (UnitedHealth/Optum and others) pushing back on rate increases and steering patients to lower-cost sites.
Nurse and physician labor shortages, union activity and wage inflation.
Shift of surgeries to lower-cost ambulatory and physician-owned sites (HCA same-facility outpatient surgeries fell 3.7% in Q3 2026).
High leverage: $50.5B of debt and a stockholders' deficit at Sept 30, 2026, after heavy buybacks.
Regulatory, antitrust and litigation risk over billing, admissions practices and market concentration.

ceo.name: Samuel N. (Sam) Hazen
ceo.background: Career HCA operator (former president of the Western Group, then President and COO from 2015); BBA University of Kentucky, MBA University of Nevada, Las Vegas

c1.evidence: HCA leads the US investor-owned hospital industry, but hospital care is a mature industry (CMS: about $1.6 trillion of US hospital spending in 2024), not an emerging one.

c2.evidence: Patients and insurers choose HCA for its dense local networks and convenience in fast-growing Sun Belt cities, an advantage built over decades that is hard to copy, but its care is not clearly different from large nonprofit rivals like AdventHealth or Baylor Scott & White.

c3.evidence: HCA is the default name among investor-owned hospital chains and its hospitals are household names locally (HCA Florida, Medical City, TriStar), but ordinary people rarely recognise the HCA parent brand or recommend it the way they do Mayo Clinic.

c4.evidence: Its mission, 'Above all else, we are committed to the care and improvement of human life,' is prominently published and repeated, but management is also strongly focused on shareholder returns (over $10B of buybacks in 2025).

c6.evidence: “big, for-profit, efficient” are the first words for many; the impression is mixed, with respect for its scale and care quality alongside criticism from unions and patient advocates about prices, staffing and profit focus.

c7.evidence: US hospital spending is about $1.6 trillion (2024, up 8.9%) and rides the secular trend of an ageing population and fast population growth in HCA's Sun Belt markets.

c8.evidence: HCA can keep expanding outpatient sites, buying hospitals and growing in the UK, but it is essentially a hospital operator with no plan to enter fundamentally new markets.

m1.evidence: Sam Hazen has a clear strategy of growing dense local networks, outpatient access and using data and AI (including a Google Cloud partnership), but he is a disciplined operator rather than a visionary.

m2.evidence: Hazen is not a founder but has spent his whole career, over 40 years, at HCA and runs it with a long-term, owner-like mindset.

m4.evidence: HCA stresses colleague programs (Galen College of Nursing, HCA Healthcare Hope Fund), but nurse unions have repeatedly criticized staffing levels at its hospitals.

m5.evidence: HCA has a strong, data-driven operating culture, but it is focused on standardized execution rather than inventing new products and technologies.

m6.evidence: Hazen is a finance-trained executive (BBA Kentucky, MBA UNLV) who rose through hospital CFO and operations roles, not an engineer or clinician.

m7.evidence: No scandals attach to Hazen personally and HCA has been named one of Ethisphere's World's Most Ethical Companies 16 times (including 2026), but the company's priorities are visibly weighted toward profit and buybacks.

m7b.evidence: No record found of Hazen giving a commencement speech at a top university; he has spoken at the University of Kentucky's Gatton College, where he is in its alumni hall of fame (2016).

m8b.evidence: Hazen keeps a low public profile and is known as a steady, numbers-focused operator rather than a memorable personality.

m9.evidence: Since he became CEO in 2019, revenue grew from $51,533M in 2020 to $75,600M in 2025 and diluted EPS from $10.93 to $28.33, helped by large buybacks that cut diluted shares from 343.6M to 239.5M.

m10.evidence: HCA is known in the industry for tight cost control and standardized supply purchasing through HealthTrust, though not for famous personal frugality.

c10.evidence: HCA treats millions of patients a year (592,179 admissions in Q3 2026 alone) and saves lives daily, but only in the US and UK, not worldwide.

p2.evidence: Running 189 hospitals safely and efficiently is hard and very important, but many other health systems do the same work.

f2.evidence: HCA reports no gross margin; net margin moved from 7.3% (2020) to a peak of 11.8% (2021), then 9.4%, 8.1%, 8.2% and 9.0% (2025), so higher than 2020 but not steadily rising.

f3.evidence: At Sept 30, 2026, debt was $50,493M against only $908M of cash, and stockholders' equity was a deficit of $(4,599)M because of large buybacks, though 2025 operating cash flow of $12,636M covers interest comfortably.

f4.evidence: Operating cash flow grew from $9,232M (2020) to $12,636M (2025) and pre-tax income from $5,430M to $9,832M, but both dipped in some years (operating cash flow fell in 2021 and 2022; pre-tax income fell in 2022 and 2023).

v1.evidence: People choose an HCA hospital mostly because it is nearby and in their insurance network, not because it is clearly better than every alternative.

v2.evidence: HCA was named one of Fortune's World's Most Admired Companies for the 12th straight year in 2026 and an Ethisphere World's Most Ethical Company 16 times, but it does not top 'best places to work' rankings and faces nurse union disputes.

c5.evidence: If HCA vanished, millions of patients in cities like Nashville, Dallas, Houston, Denver and much of Florida would lose their nearest emergency rooms and hospitals, overwhelming other providers.
